newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore leaders win record damages from foe.
newsitem.headline: Singapore leaders win record damages from foe.

text.p: A Singapore court awarded Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and senior colleagues in his ruling party a record Singapore $8.08 million (US$5.65 million) in libel damages on Thursday after a political foe called them liars.

Justice Chao Hick Tin said Goh and his colleagues were justified in calling opposition politician Tang Liang Hong "an anti-English education, anti-Christian Chinese chauvinist" who was a danger to Singapore's racial harmony.

Tang had made "malicious" attacks on Goh, former prime minister Lee Kuan Yew and the others which could have affected "their moral authority to govern", including calling them liars over the chauvinism charge, Chao said in a written judgment.

Goh and his People's Action Party (PAP) colleagues had demanded aggravated damages totalling S$12.9 million, saying Tang had continued to defame them in media interviews he gave after fleeing Singapore saying he had received death threats.
Tang, who fled to the south Malaysian state of Johor after losing a bitterly contested general election fight in January, to Reuters that he would appeal against the damages.
"Surely I am not satisfied with this because to me they are not entitled to one cent," Tang said by telephone from Hong Kong.
Tang said he intended to bring in a top British lawyer to argue his case but that the costs of his appeal were mounting as now he had to deposit S$5,000 for each case to cover costs.
"This is not a legal battle, rather this is a test of financial strength. Now I have got financial problem. I cannot keep on borrowing. Who would lend it to me like that?"
Tang lost the libel cases in March by failing to turn up to defend himself against charges which mounted almost every time he spoke to the media from Johor, London and Hong Kong.

The comments for which he was sued included an interview with Singapore's Straits Times newspaper, which reported that he claimed "the suits were being used as a politican weapon to squeeze him out of the political area and to 'bury him politically and financially'".
"It is clear that the above quoted remarks constituted another grave attack" on Goh, Lee and their colleagues, Justice Chao said. He made it clear that such comments justified aggravated damages.
"This court must show its indignation at the injury inflicted on the plaintiffs," he said. "It cannot be disputed that in terms of aggravation, these 13 cases have no equal."
"The more enormous, outrageous, scandalous or scurrilous the defamation, and/or aggravation, the greater the damages," he added.
Goh, involved in three of the suits against Tang, was awarded S$1.4 million. Lee, involved in five, won the biggest amount -- S$2.3 million.
Chao hinted that there could be further action against Tang, who was heavily criticised by judges for his manoevering during a rash of court hearings leading up to the damages award.
"Whether Mr Tang should be dealt with for scandalising the courts is a matter which may have to be taken up at some other time," Chao said.
Tang was also formally charged last Friday with 33 counts of tax evasion. The court issued an arrest warrant for him.
Tang faces a fine of three times the amount of tax he is accused of evading -- S$211,000 -- plus a fine of S$10,000 on each charge. He could also be jailed for three years on each charge.
